paragraphs.text: God has very great pleasure in things that are complete. When God begins to do something He never leaves it unfinished. Very often we do, but God never does. If God, so to speak, reaches out to do something, He pursues it and continues it with a patience that is all His own until finally what He set out to do is done. He spoke in regard of creation “and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast”, Psalm 33: 9. There is eloquent testimony as to the perfection of what God did in the minute and accurate manner in which things in the creation work, so much so that men must of necessity make their calculations in regard to calculations that God has already made.

So I want to speak of things that God finds great pleasure in that are complete, and, in speaking about them, I would like the impact of the truth to find an answer in all our hearts. I speak first of our Lord Jesus Christ. There was never ever any need that anything should be completed in Him; there was perfection in detail in relation to the position that He took in manhood, but there were things that He put His hand to that were completed by Him. In us there are things that need to be completed, but it was never so with Jesus. We need to hold the truth as to His Person inviolate, to let no thought or suggestion in any sense detract from the perfection of His Person, because that perfection gives character to everything that He put His hand to do. Let us remember that.

In John 17, in speaking to His Father, it is clear that a certain great work was committed into the hands of Jesus. Primarily that work was in relation to the will of God, that God might be glorified, that God might be honoured, that there might be something secured for God in people like you and me that would glorify Him and honour Him. Jesus, so to speak, unreservedly committed Himself to this work that He undertook to do as Man for God. What pleasure God had in Him! What a wonderful study John’s gospel is in relation to those links of perfect affection between the Father and the Son, so that the Son always glorifies the Father and relates everything to the Father; moves with the prerogative that is His because of who He is, but moves as Man in relation to the Father. What glory that is!

So in John 17 we have this profound and blessed insight into what those relationships were and what kind of communications went on in those relationships. Why should God allow us, so to speak, to listen to what Jesus said to Him? Why should the Father be pleased to let us into the secret of love’s conversations? I believe it is to give us an understanding of how Jesus was here in the glory of manhood. In Luke’s gospel it is the dependence of manhood; I believe the glory of manhood is in John’s gospel. And so it says. He “lifted up his eyes to heaven and said, Father, the hour is come; glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee”.

When He said that He was on the threshold of Calvary, already committed to that mighty work that would for ever resolve for God everything that stood athwart His pleasure and His purpose and His desires for man in relation to Himself.

And so Jesus says, “I have glorified thee on the earth, I have completed the work which thou gavest me that I should do it”. He had not yet been crucified, and it required the crucifixion, His death, to complete that work, but He says this in anticipation of that; He looks on, so to speak, as having committed Himself fully and irrevocably—He could not draw back and He would not draw back (impossible that He should) from completing the work that was given Him to do.

How vast is the extent of it! How detailed that which was involved! Redemption’s work was involved in it; the fulfilment of God’s will in regard of what He purposed; then too the setting aside of an order of things that could never ever yield pleasure to God and the bringing in in Christ of another order of things in which God would be honoured now and for ever.

I love the thought that God is honoured now in virtue of what Christ has done. Of course, it does raise the question as to whether I am in it; whether I take advantage of what Christ has done. You say, How may I take advantage? Put implicit confidence in Him. Throw everything else aside, and put implicit confidence in Him, and once you open your heart to Christ with implicit confidence what you get is all that He is, and all that He has done. Do you believe that? Thank God if you do! Then I say, Give place to Him in your soul. Without the shadow of a doubt it will alter every facet of your life. It will! What you do will in measure be like what Jesus did. What did He do? He considered for God with utter disregard to self. You say, That tests me. It tests me too; I confess that. We are measured in relation to God’s standard and I think something like that happens as we speak together about these wonderful, holy realities. Jesus considered for God with utter disregard for Himself. What a standard, is it not?

The Spirit of God would help us as He points out the satisfaction that God has in what is complete. “I have completed the work which thou gavest me that I should do it; and now glorify me, thou Father, along with thyself, with the glory which I had along with thee before the world was”. That verse carries something of the inscrutable glory of the Person of Christ, who He is. It is wonderful to think of the glory that He had along with the Father before the world was—that would be the glory of the Deity and He speaks about that in the hearing of people who could pass it on to you and me. Glorified He is indeed! The glory of Jesus is the witness to the complete satisfaction that God has in the work that was given Him to do. Let us keep that in our hearts; let us hold that in our minds, that Jesus is not on the cross, that He is glorified, and the glory of Christ is the witness of God’s satisfaction in the work that He has done. You say, ‘I believe in Him’. Then the value of that work is yours. You say, ‘I put my confidence in Him’. Then all that He is is yours.
‘Oh’, you say, ‘God delights in him’. Yes, and He delights in every person whom He places

“in Christ Jesus”. You may say, ‘But I do not feel ...’. It is not a question of feeling; it is a question of believing. Do you believe? These are the wonderful facts of God’s glad tidings, and the facts are presented that we might believe. The Holy Spirit is given to confirm us in our consciousness that what we believe is indeed a reality.

The apostle Paul, in writing to these Philippians thanked God for them, and what he recognised was this, that God had begun in them a good work, and what was more. Paul, who had a peculiar link with these believers in Philippi, had confidence that what God had begun He would complete. Now we have that confidence too. I would like to inspire confidence in every person here. I would like to inspire confidence in every company of saints who gather in the light of the assembly, who seek to walk in that light, that He who has begun is He who will complete.

It would be unreasonable, would it not, to think otherwise? And where is the work done? It is done in the souls of persons. It is not done by organising; it is not done by agreement; it is not done even because certain great items of the truth are subscribed to by people and they say, ‘I believe this and you believe that too, therefore we can be together’. It is not done like that. It is done in the souls of people, and God operates by His Spirit, and His Spirit delights to magnify Christ.

“He who has begun in you a good work will complete it unto Jesus Christ’s day”; that is why I say the Spirit delights to glorify Christ. Where does He do it? Where does He make much of Christ? In your heart and in mine. Something happens in people when they give Christ the full place in their hearts. It is not outward glory, that is going to be seen in Jesus Christ’s day.

Yet people do see something now. In John 9 the neighbours saw that the man who had his eyes opened was different. But there is coming a day, and it is cherished in the hearts of those who believe in Jesus and who have had their sins forgiven because He died and bore the judgment for them, when the One who was despised—and is still despised and rejected of men—is going to be honoured and glorified in the presence of men. Do you rejoice in that? I find a thrill goes through my soul every time I think about it. There is a verse which says—
this—
‘Thee, my Master and my Friend,
Vindicated and enthroned,
Unto earth’s remotest end
Glorified, adored and owned’.
Does that not thrill you?—that God is working, operating powerfully, in people, right inside their beings, helping them to appreciate the One in whom

His pleasure is centred, who completed the work that He gave Him to do. God is working by His Spirit in persons at the present time, and what is so establishing and assuring is that He who has begun a good work in you—not by you—will complete it. You know, there are people who think that christianity is doing good to other people. Of course, that comes into it, but it is not the real test of christianity. The real test of christianity is what God is doing in people. So it says, “He who has begun in you a good work will complete it unto Jesus Christ’s day”.

Then, I say, He is working at the present time. Not only did He work in Philippi, He is working now He is working in Chelmsford. Name the place where there are persons who seek to walk in the light of the assembly—God is working that there may be an expression of what is of the assembly there. Moreover we can be sure that in whomsoever He works, or wherever He works. He is working to completion in relation to what He has in mind to do.

There is a scripture in the Old Testament which says that when they bring forth the headstone of the house they bring it forth with shoutings; “Grace, grace unto it!”, Zechariah 4: 7. That is the top-stone. They had come up from the foundations, right through the edifice, and the headstone was put on it. Who is that? It is Christ. And who is the foundation? It is Christ. The completion is the same as the foundation. So God is working to the top-stone, to the completion, and it is in view of that wonderful day of display.

The apostle Paul was committed to God’s work and he laboured more than all. He was picked up by a divine intervention, he was commissioned, and he fulfilled what was given him to do with a zeal that was commensurate with his appreciation of the grace
that had intervened on his behalf. He speaks of himself as the chief of sinners and if he is chief, everyone else is behind, so there is hope for everyone. “Less than the least of all saints”

(Ephesians 3: 8), that is how he speaks of himself; but he committed himself to that great service for God, and he committed himself to complete what had been given him to do. God finds pleasure in that. You say, ‘Oh, he was special’. He was special; but this scripture is most encouraging because I believe that it would help us to see that where there is in any sense committal in relation to God and to the Lord Jesus Christ. God finds pleasure in that being pursued and worked out to an end.
So the apostle says, “For I am already being poured out”; he was going to die, but not like any other man. He was going to die in relation to the God whom he had served. He was being

“poured out as a libation” (Philippians 2: 17)—that is, a drink offering. Paul says, “The time of my release is come”. He also says how much better it is to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1: 23). He did not have an easy time in fulfilling what was given him to do, but he says, “I have combated the good combat, I have finished the race”. He kept going, and he kept going until the course was complete. He did not drop out half-way. You see that very often in a cross-country race some drop out; others keep going steadily until they complete the course. That is the idea. These simple illustrations are of great spiritual value. “I have combated the good combat, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith”. How did he do it?

He kept his eye on the Lord in glory and relied upon the Spirit. How shall we do it? In the same way. It is very simple; it is very real. You see, christianity is not a theory; it is a thing to be worked out in the lives of people who have proved the blessedness of what it is to be in touch with God in the working out of matters.

So Paul says, “Henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will render to me in that day; but not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing”. Not ‘a’ crown, but ‘the crown’. The crown that Paul gets in character is the same crown as that rendered to others. Who are those who love His appearing? They are those who recognise that the place that belongs to Christ is the place of absolute supremacy. How do they manifest it? They give Him that place now in their own hearts. You could not say that you loved His appearing, could you, and then go and do your own will? How could you say that? You would not be true. You would not be a man or woman marked by reality. Those who love His appearing are those who recognise that He is to have the supreme place, and give it to Him now. The apostle went on that line and he completed his course in a way that glorified God. Well, I should like to be on that line, would not you? I would like to be engaged with the Man who finished the work that God gave Him to do, that glorious Man. I would like to be among those in whom God is working, working to completion, that He might have that for Himself that satisfies Him. What is that? A real expression of what the assembly is in the places where God has set us. You say, ‘Is it possible?’. You walk in that light and something will come into expression that characteristically is of the assembly. God has His delight in that.

I commend those few thoughts to us; they are fragmentary, but I desire that every person in this hall might be concerned to know the Lord Jesus, to honour Him, to be governed by Him, to put themselves in the way of blessing and go on to completion. Is there anybody here who feels they would like to give up? I hope not! Do not give up! Go on! You will find that the Spirit of God Himself will help you because God delights in completion. May God bless his word.

articles.title: DEPENDENCE AND JUDGMENT
articles.author: J. Renton
articles.place: Substance of word in meeting for ministry, Victoria, B.C.

paragraphs.text: The Lord Jesus said as Man here, “I cannot do anything of myself”. He was the One who created the universe, by whom God made the worlds (Hebrews 1: 2). We think of the greatness of His Person and then read a verse like this, and we wonder. It shows the place the Lord took as Man here; the place He took in the divine economy. He came into the place of subjection and obedience as a Man here. If the Lord Jesus was here in dependence, how necessary for us that we should be dependent. I have been impressed by the thought that the setting in which the Lord was here in relation to His Father is the setting in which we are to be in relation to the Lord when He is absent. If the Lord could say “I cannot do anything of myself”, we have to learn how much more true it ought to be of us! The Lord said in chapter 15: 5, “without me ye can do nothing”. As believers we have to learn what dependence is.

If there is one thing we need, dear brethren, it is the element of judgment. Judgment here is righteous—“as I hear, I judge”. As He heard from His Father, He judged. We need to know what right judgment is; it involves discernment and discrimination. We need to know first of all how to judge ourselves. We speak about self-judgment, but that is not having our own standard. We are to regulate ourselves by His word. The word of God is living and operative (Hebrews 4: 12). It divides between soul and spirit. It is in allowing God’s word to have its effect in our very inwards that we are able to judge ourselves and to judge other things. The Lord speaks of judgment on a moral basis—“I do not seek my will, but the will of him that has sent me”. We need to be fully committed to the will of God to have a right judgment. The Lord therefore is a perfect example for us. There was no element of preference or prejudice with Him, but these things come in and affect our judgment. There was never anyone so single-eyed as the Lord Jesus. He never deviated from God’s will. He was ever in perfection devoted to God’s will. We do well to feed on Him and be occupied with Him. It is so different from men around us in the world. The believer is meant to be devoted to the will of God.

The verses read in John 7 are a challenge to the believer as to whether he is governed by anything else but to practise God’s will. It could be linked with Romans 7: 25; “So then I myself with the mind serve God’s law”. This is the inward man operating. The believer’s judgment so often is affected by preference or prejudice. The Spirit will help us to practise God’s will as He is the unction. The believer has a sense of what is right and wrong by having the unction. How good to repudiate every other influence and to practise His will.

Then we will get a sense of what is right and wrong. This belongs to believers as having the Holy Spirit, but whether He is allowed to function is another matter. The desire to practise God’s will would allow the unction to operate and give us sensibilities which are of the Spirit.

The preaching of the gospel has a number of results in mind. God’s glad tidings meets the need of every sinner, however great that need may be, and one of the pleasures God has in hearing His glad tidings preached is that His beloved Son is well spoken of. Though all present are christians and may have been on the road many years we each need the gospel, I am sure of that.

As we know, John in his gospel records for us more of the words of Jesus than the other gospel writers. I have been struck by the fact that he records the Lord as saying, “I am the light of the world”, “I am the good shepherd”, and other references of that kind. I would that the Spirit might help us get a fresh touch from these verses so that the reality of what is presented in Christ may freshly affect our souls. In, each of these presentations there is not only what the Lord says He is, but some result is in view in all who accept the word. No one can say ‘I am’ like Jesus could say it. Later in chapter 8 the opposers of the Lord say, “Who art thou?” (John 8: 25). “Jesus said to them, Altogether that which I also say to you”. There is a footnote to the word “altogether”—‘in the principle and universality of what I am; that is, His speech presented Himself, being the truth’. It conveys this to us, that whatever Christ says He is, He is that absolutely and perfectly.

His servant, the apostle Paul, could say, “By God’s grace I am what I am” (1 Corinthians 15: 10): God had worked in him and some result was visible in the apostle; and in every believer there should be some substantial result so that we might be able to say, like the apostle, I am what I am by God’s grace.
But when Jesus says, “I am the light of the world”, this is something distinctive and absolute.

One recalls that He does say to His disciples, “Ye are the light of the world” (Matthew 5: 14), and that would need to be understood in its own connection. But this is something said by the Lord and recorded by John that no one else could ever say—“I am the light of the world”. I think it is very wonderful to have presented to us a Person who says, without the slightest possibility of contradiction, “I am the light of the world”. Earlier in the gospel John has spoken of “the true light ... which coming into the world, lightens every man” (John l: 9). It shines upon all.

It is wonderful to take account of God’s disposition as presented in His beloved Son. He is toward all, and the light of the world, which Christ is, is shining for everybody. Not everybody, alas, gets the gain of it, but the light is shining for all. “I am the light of the world”—and no one needs to exclude himself from the benefit of this glorious light that is shining in Jesus. It was shining when He was here and it is shining still. The apostle Paul speaks of the glory of God shining in the face of Jesus Christ (see 2 Corinthians 4: 6). So what a blessed thing it is to be able to speak of a Person who is the light of the world. How thankful we are to know One who has brought such light to us so that we understand and get an illumination of the facts that bear upon time and eternity. It is what the world needs, what persons in the world need; the light shines in that blessed Person: “I am the light of the world; he that follows me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life”.

Now this is a very blessed promise. If people listen to the words of Jesus, if people accept what God presents in His own beloved Son, they receive the light in their hearts so that they no longer walk in darkness but have the light of life. We live in a world with death and moral degradation all around us, and it is wonderful that this light is still shining. We can well afford to listen attentively to Jesus when He says, “I am the light of the world”. As we listen to Him, as we see the truth of His word, it sets us upon a path no longer in darkness but in light. I speak to persons who know this, who have followed Him as the light of the world and are walking in the light of life, but it is always refreshing just to go over some of our blessings, what Christ means to us, that the light has shone into our hearts so that we are brought into a sphere of things that is marked by the light of life. That is a wonderful thing, that we are no longer in darkness as to God, but we know him and realise what a God He is because Jesus has made Him known to us.

In John 10 the Lord says, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep”. How we long that persons might hear Jesus saying, “I am the good shepherd”, that they might receive His word and come into the benefit of all that He would be to them as having laid down His life for them. Oh how much is involved in that! One thinks of the feelings of Jesus as He said, “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep”. What love was behind these words, for He knew what was involved in laying down His life. How much was involved! It meant His going to the cross, being taken by wicked hands and crucified and slain. And there on the cross He bore the judgment, the judgment

due to the sheep. How glad we are to hear these words from His lips afresh, because they are as true now as when He first uttered them and John recorded them for us: “I am the good shepherd”. We speak now in the light of that great work having been done; He has laid down His life for the sheep. Oh how we thank Him for it! Every one who realises that the good Shepherd has laid down His life for the sheep is glad to hear afresh the words of Jesus, “I am the good shepherd”.

Then later in the chapter He says, “I am the good shepherd; and I know those that are mine, and am known of those that are mine, as the Father knows me and I know the Father; and I lay down my life for the sheep” (John 10: 14, 15). Think of the personal link that Jesus has with every believer. He knows every one, and He is known of them, every one of them. How is it that we have this personal link with the Saviour? We know by faith that He is a Man ascended. The work, the laying down of His life, is completed, blessedly completed in all its fulness. What it meant to the blessed God that Jesus laid down His life, that he bore on the cross God’s judgment on account of our sins. His precious blood was shed, His life given up, and He lay in the grave, there for us, so that what was offensive is entirely removed from the sight of a holy God. He rose from the dead and is now ascended; we know by faith a glorious Man at God’s right hand, and from there He has sent down the Holy Spirit to indwell the hearts of believers. How precious that is! But then as He says, “I know those that are mine, and am known of those that are mine”. He assures us afresh in the preaching of the word today that every one who puts his trust in Him has a personal attachment to Him, and He gives the Spirit to indwell the heart so that we have an immediate link with the Man in the glory.

There are quite a number of these references. In chapter 10 Jesus says, “I am the door” (John 10: 7); and in chapter 6 (which has been called the great constitutional chapter in John’s gospel), “I am the bread of life” (John 6: 48); how much could be said as to that. But I go on to John 11—“I am the resurrection and the life”. These words were true when He said them to Martha, but they are true today, and this is most reassuring to every believer. No one else, no other man, could say such words, and they result in Martha believing; and the gospel is preached that persons might believe. As we have often commented, John’s gospel is written that believers might believe (see John 20: 31).

Martha at the first says, “If thou hadst been here, my brother had not died; but even now I know, that whatsoever thou shalt ask of God, God will give thee” (John 11: 22). Her words sound very pious, but what she is completely overlooking is that the Person there was God Himself. Jesus had said earlier in the gospel, “Unless ye shall believe that I am he, ye shall die in your sins” (John 8: 24). Solemn word! Martha regarded Him as any other man that would have liberty to ask God for something and He would grant it. But the Lord meets that in these powerful words—“I am the resurrection and the life”; that is, He personally is the resurrection and the life. He has the power over death. What a mighty triumphant Saviour is ours! He has been into death and triumphed over it. What a victory He has secured! and He has “set free all those who through fear of death through the whole of their life were subject to bondage”, Hebrews 2: 15. I say, what a victory to know One who is the resurrection, who has the power over death and hades, our glorious Saviour! And He is still saying today, “I am the resurrection and the life”.
What a comfort it is to us, in all the circumstances

through which we pass, to realise that our blessed Saviour is the resurrection and the life, and we can depend upon Him absolutely—if we believe on Him. The Lord says, “I am the resurrection and the life—he that believes on me, though he have died, shall live”. Well, that is very wonderful! As we think of the myriads of believers who have died since these words were spoken it reminds us of what Paul says, “The dead in Christ shall rise first”, 1 Thessalonians 4: 16. There will not be one missing, because all will hear the voice of the Son of God, the One who says, “I am the resurrection and the life”. He is the One who is able to raise the dead in Christ and give them life. “And every one who lives and believes on me shall never die”—what does that mean? I suppose it would apply to every believer living when the Lord comes for us. That may be, as we know, so soon; it may be tonight. Oh how great the Person we know! How glorious a Man is Jesus! a real Man and yet in His Person over all, God blessed for ever. He who is God in His Person has effected for man the work that needed to be done so that souls might be saved for time and eternity.

Oh how our hearts are drawn out to the One who could say, “I am the light of the world”; “I am the good shepherd”; “I am the resurrection and the life”. I think this would be specially comforting to us as we just let Jesus say these words afresh to us. We heard announced this morning the burial of a beloved brother tomorrow, but then, “I am the resurrection and the life”. This is intended to comfort and sustain us in all the vicissitudes of our walk here and in all that is involved in the testimony, He will bring everything through; His sheep have an eternal link with Him; He knows every one, and they know Him. What a beautiful link, as it says, “as the Father knows me and I know the Father”. What a standard of relation and affection there is between the sheep and the Shepherd!

As I said earlier, there is a consequence resulting from answering to the truth presented by Jesus in these words as John records them for us. So Jesus says to Thomas, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”. It seems to me to imply that everything we need we have in Him.
But the point here particularly is the link with the Father, access to the Father—“No one comes to the Father unless by me”. That is a very blessed thing, to know God as our Father.

Then how is it that we can have liberty to address God as our Father? We come to the Father by Christ. What we need in order to be at home in the presence of the Father, we have in this glorious Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ—“I am the way, and the truth, and the life”.

For myself I would just like to go over these words and get some fuller understanding of them. “I am the way”; I think we can understand that a little; Jesus has gone to the Father and He has prepared there a place for us, as He says in the beginning of this chapter—“In my Father’s house there are many abodes … I go to prepare you a place; and if I go and shall prepare you a place, I am coming again and shall receive you to myself, that where I am ye also may be”. So we can see that He is the way into all the blessedness that christianity involves for believers. It is something to be enjoyed now because the Spirit has been given to us; something to be entered into finally, which verse three refers to—“I am coming again and shall receive you to myself, that where I am ye also may be”. We have no doubt about it because we have listened to the words of Jesus and we accept them as He says, “I am the way”.

Then, “I am … the truth”—all that can be known of God is presented in that blessed Man. So we can be at home in the light of God because we know One who is not only the way but is the truth and the life, the means by which believers find life in the presence of the Father.

I commend these references in John to each of us and I would like to go over them too myself because I feel there is a fulness in them which we have hardly touched at this time. There is something very choice in what the Lord says—“I am the light of the world”; “I am the good shepherd”; “I am the resurrection and the life”, and “I am the way, and the truth, and the life”.
How blessed to know Him thus! May God bless the word.

We have read about three persons who made decisions. Life is made up of making decisions and sometimes, as in Acts 16, important consequences hang on making a right one. Every decision in a believer’s life is important, enough to refer to God for direction. God has given us a brain and a measure of common sense, but He loves to be invited into a believer’s life and to be consulted about his affairs. Of course, He sometimes comes in even if He is not invited. One has also heard of fathers in a gathering inviting the north wind into their
localities, because they saw the need for some element of discipline to counter the damage that was developing through material prosperity and which was tending to carry all away.
You would need to be very spiritual to do that. Yet the Lord in His love for us sometimes comes in when we have not asked Him, to discipline us; that is His matter and He has a right to do it.

I have read firstly about Lot, who had gone up with Abram out of Haran. Lot, like many of us, had had the benefit and privilege of the company of a spiritual man, but there came a time when he was faced with a decision of his own. He had been down to Egypt previously and it seems that the world had somewhat damaged his soul. We are in the world but, so as not to be damaged, we need to keep clear of the influence and the principles which govern it. But it seems the world had had some effect on Lot so that when Abram gave him this choice he was confused. He confused the garden of Jehovah with the land of Egypt. The world is not the garden of Jehovah, yet many a believer sets himself to make his world the garden of Jehovah.

This tendency may be nearer to us than we think. Many an earnest soul in christendom cherishes the outlook that the millennium will come about through the gospel being preached and the world being converted, but it is not the truth. Lot made his choice, and alas it was the wrong one.

Every word in Scripture is meaningful, so perhaps the key to his wrong decision lies in the fact that ‘he chose for himself’; it seems that he did not discuss the matter with his uncle or ask his advice, nor does it seem that he prayed about it. Something appealed to him naturally, and things may appeal to us. Perhaps you have already made up your mind before you have carried a matter into the Lord’s presence. How important then to lay out every matter in prayer to the Lord first, for you cannot say anything to Him which is not the truth. You may delude yourself, but the great safeguard is to tell Him all about your problem, all your fears and doubts, and you will find that things will become much clearer in your own mind. It does not seem that Lot did that. The world is alluring and Lot saw this well-watered plain and chose it, yet shortly afterwards it was to be covered with dust and ashes. Jude (Jude 7) says it lies there as an example for us. Poor Lot! he had made the wrong choice. What a warning to us as to not reckoning with God. We should shrink from doing anything without considering how God views it.

Now Mary also made a choice, and I would like her choice to be ours. I do not wish to speak against Martha because, when you think about it, she had quite a lot on hand. I expect all the disciples were there and so in a way it is understandable that Martha was distracted. It is so easy to be distracted in a meeting. A baby cries, and everyone looks round—well, babies have been crying for years; there is nothing exceptional about it. So it is not only Martha, but you and I who can be distracted. Mary, however, quite deliberately chose to sit at the Lord’s feet. The attitude of her mind was to want to listen to what the Lord had to say. Put the distractions out of your mind for a moment and sit at the Lord’s feet and learn the deepest lessons. A hymn writer said—
‘Low at Thy feet, Lord Jesus,
This is the place for me;
Here I have learned deep lessons,
Truth that has set me free’.

You and I, like Mary, can have this privilege of sitting at the feet of the greatest Instructor that ever was. The way to learn is to be subject and ready to receive His words. Schools are not noted nowadays for students sitting at the feet of the instructor; rather the opposite, for the spirit of rebellion is never far away. In the divine system the way to learn is to sit at the Lord’s feet and listen to His word. The Lord commends that.

The Lord will, sometimes in most unexpected ways, speak to you in a meeting about your personal matters. It is therefore worth listening on that account, for He may say something which just bears on the situation facing you at the moment. This was not exactly the case with Mary, for she was listening to His word for its own sake. I am sure the Lord Jesus greatly appreciates anyone who is interested in His affairs. He loves to see someone who does not want to dash out into the playground as soon as the school bell goes at the end of the lesson, but who will stay and ask a question. The Lord enters feelingly and sympathetically into every circumstance, and I am sure the saints in their measure endeavour to do so too. But whatever the circumstance, the Lord loves us to stay and listen to His word, to glean the truth and rejoice in it. He says she “has chosen the good part, the which shall not be taken from her”. In the breaks between the meetings we have the joy of conversing to one another and keeping abreast of what the Lord may be doing here and there, which is valuable in its place, but I trust that we ever remember that the greatest thing is to listen to His word. If we listen, He will continue to supply it. No doubt Martha listened the next time, for in John 12 it just says “and Martha served”.

When Moses ‘became great’ may mean ‘when he became someone of note in Egypt’; but I would first like to take up this passage as it is translated in the Authorised Version, which is, “when he was come to years”. Mr. Taylor said this meant that he was mature. This raises the exercise with me as to whether I am mature and whether I am growing in my appreciation of divine things. I feel sure that many brethren are more mature than I am, but I would like to be growing. As the, weeks go by we all ought to know more about our inheritance. When Moses was grown he was prepared to refuse to be called son of Pharaoh’s daughter and to choose to suffer affliction. Had he been governed by his circumstances his choice would have been different. It comes back to what we were saying in the reading that, if you look at what is all around, that will tend to colour your judgment; but if you look at the truth and all that God has done, that will govern you. Which way will it be with you? As being governed by the truth, Moses made his choice and he cast in his lot with an afflicted people under reproach and suffering. In people under such circumstances he nevertheless saw features that were going to shine in glory. When the affliction, the weakness and the confusion have all gone, the features of glory in every believer on the Lord Jesus will shine.

Every feature will then reflect Christ and there will be no trace of anything else. There is that which is going through and we need to look ahead, like Moses, and not be ashamed of being identified with a suffering and afflicted people.

In certain newspapers there is a column called the ‘Court Circular’ which gives news about the high-ups of the land. What a stir would have been caused when the equivalent of the Court Circular in Egypt announced that Moses was refusing to be called son of Pharaoh’s daughter; but he had made his choice and it was a right one. What helped him to make that choice? No doubt the faith and prayers of his parents who had in type had him baptised lay behind it, just as the prayers of brethren and parents have been the preservation of many of us, but we cannot ignore personal responsibility. Moses made a right choice—you and I too have a responsibility to make right decisions.

Even if Lot made a wrong choice, it is encouraging to read of two who made right ones. If I am the one who has made a wrong choice, let me now start to make right ones. There is no reason why we should make mistakes. Through weakness we do make mistakes, and we need to plead as priests for one another so as to strengthen one another in order that weakness might not remain and become characteristic. The Lord is very gracious, of course, but He does love to be consulted, and we do need always to bring Him into all our circumstances.

Well, may we make right decisions. We do not know what it will be about, but let the next choice be a right one. If we have that before us, the Lord will help us and we shall be blessed in answering to His claims. May it be so, for His name’s sake.

I have been lately very much interested in the simple fact that we belong to heaven, and that “such as the heavenly one, such also the heavenly ones”. We are only on a journey to our new place where the Object of our heart is, and where we shall be in full harmony with His pleasure. Everything there is in accordance with His will. Why do we not more seek the things which are above?
